q: Mechanisms of breathing are for gas exchange which is the uptake of oxygen from environment and the elimination of carbon dioxide from the body.
e: True. Mechanisms of breathing are for gas exchange which is the uptake of oxygen from environment and the elimination of carbon dioxide from the body. Carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis and produced by respiration and combustion. Gas exchange is uptake of oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide.

q: Mechanisms of breathing are for gas exchange which is the uptake of carbon dioxide from environment and the elimination of oxygen from the body.
e: False. Mechanisms of breathing are for gas exchange which is not the uptake of carbon dioxide from environment and the elimination of oxygen from the body. Carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis and produced by respiration and combustion. Gas exchange is uptake of oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide.

q: The general body surface of most animals lacks sufficient surface area to exchange gases for the whole organism.
e: True. The general body surface of most animals lacks sufficient surface area to exchange gases for the whole organism. A large surface area speeds diffusion, which is why lungs, gills, and leaves are folded or flattened.

q: Respiratory or breathing organs are extensively folded or branched thereby reducing the available surface area for gas exchange.
e: False. It is not true that respiratory or breathing organs are extensively folded or branched thereby reducing the available surface area for gas exchange. Gas exchange is uptake of oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide. A large surface area speeds diffusion, which is why lungs, gills, and leaves are folded or flattened.

q: Gills are gas exchange organs for aquatic animals.
e: True. Gills are gas exchange organs for aquatic animals. Gas exchange is uptake of oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide. Gills are folded, water-suspended surfaces used by many aquatic animals.

q: Aquatic turtles use gills for gas exchange.
e: False. It is not true that aquatic turtles use gills for gas exchange. Gas exchange is uptake of oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide. Gills are folded, water-suspended surfaces used by many aquatic animals.

q: Each gill arch has two rows of gill filaments, composed of flattened plates called lamellae.
e: True. Each gill arch has two rows of gill filaments, composed of flattened plates called lamellae. Dichotomous means divided into two parts, from Greek.

q: The counter current flow of water and blood causes the continuous diffusion of oxygen from the water into the blood over the entire length of a capillary.
e: True. The counter current flow of water and blood causes the continuous diffusion of oxygen from the water into the blood over the entire length of a capillary. Blood carries oxygen bound to haemoglobin. Counter-current flow in fish gills keeps a gradient so more oxygen is extracted.

q: Although the most familiar respiratory structure among terrestrial animals is the lungs, some use tracheae in insects.
e: True. Although the most familiar respiratory structure among terrestrial animals is the lungs, some use tracheae in insects. Many insects breathe through a tracheal system, not lungs. Lungs are the main terrestrial organs of gas exchange.

q: Spiders and scorpions use skin for respiration.
e: False. It is not true that spiders and scorpions use skin for respiration. Respiration releases energy from food; do not mix it up with just breathing. Skin is a surface for some heat exchange and a barrier, but most large animals also need lungs or gills.

q: Frogs and toads often use the lining of the buccal cavity for gas exchange.
e: True. Frogs and toads often use the lining of the buccal cavity for gas exchange. Gas exchange is uptake of oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide.

q: The lungs are enclosed in the chest or thorax by the rib cage and a muscular sheet of tissue called the diaphragm.
e: True. The lungs are enclosed in the chest or thorax by the rib cage and a muscular sheet of tissue called the diaphragm. The diaphragm contracts and flattens to increase thorax volume during inhalation. Lungs are the main terrestrial organs of gas exchange.

q: The diaphragm separates the contents of the thorax from the pelvis.
e: False. It is not true that the diaphragm separates the contents of the thorax from the pelvis. The diaphragm contracts and flattens to increase thorax volume during inhalation.

q: The diaphragm is flat, with a fibrous middle part forming the roof of the dome.
e: False. It is not true that the diaphragm is flat, with a fibrous middle part forming the roof of the dome. The diaphragm contracts and flattens to increase thorax volume during inhalation.

q: The air passages of the lungs form a highly branching network, which is why it is sometimes called the bronchial tree.
e: True. The air passages of the lungs form a highly branching network, which is why it is sometimes called the bronchial tree. Lungs are the main terrestrial organs of gas exchange.

q: The trachea splits into two tubes called the bronchi, one leading to each lung.
e: True. The trachea splits into two tubes called the bronchi, one leading to each lung. The trachea is the airway that carries air toward the bronchi. Dichotomous means divided into two parts, from Greek.

q: Each bronchus divides into smaller and smaller tubes called alveoli, eventually ending at microscopic air sacs called bronchioles.
e: False. It is not true that each bronchus divides into smaller and smaller tubes called alveoli, eventually ending at microscopic air sacs called bronchioles. Bronchioles are the finer airways that end in alveoli. Alveoli are tiny lung sacs with a huge surface for diffusion of gases.

q: The walls of trachea and bronchi contain rings of gristle or cartilage to support the airway and keep them open when breathing.
e: True. The walls of trachea and bronchi contain rings of gristle or cartilage to support the airway and keep them open when breathing. Cartilage keeps airways such as the trachea open. The trachea is the airway that carries air toward the bronchi.

q: The inside of the thorax is separated from the lungs by two thin, moist membranes called the pleural membranes.
e: True. The inside of the thorax is separated from the lungs by two thin, moist membranes called the pleural membranes. Pleural membranes and fluid let the lungs slide as the thorax changes volume. Lungs are the main terrestrial organs of gas exchange.

q: Between the two pleural membranes is a space called the pleural cavity, filled with a thin layer of liquid called pleural fluid which acts as lubrication.
e: True. Between the two pleural membranes is a space called the pleural cavity, filled with a thin layer of liquid called pleural fluid which acts as lubrication. Pleural membranes and fluid let the lungs slide as the thorax changes volume. Dichotomous means divided into two parts, from Greek.

q: The trachea acts as a site for the exchange of gases.
e: False. It is not true that the trachea acts as a site for the exchange of gases. The trachea is the airway that carries air toward the bronchi.

q: Some cells in the lining of trachea and bronchi secrete mucus which traps particles of dirt or bacteria that are breathed in.
e: True. Some cells in the lining of trachea and bronchi secrete mucus which traps particles of dirt or bacteria that are breathed in. The trachea is the airway that carries air toward the bronchi. Mucus traps particles; cilia sweep that dirt away from the lungs.

q: Cilia on cells lining the trachea and bronchi secrete mucus to trap particles.
e: False. It is not true that cilia on cells lining the trachea and bronchi secrete mucus to trap particles. The trachea is the airway that carries air toward the bronchi. Mucus traps particles; cilia sweep that dirt away from the lungs.

q: Pleural membranes separate the inside of the thorax from the lungs and secrete the pleural fluid.
e: True. Pleural membranes separate the inside of the thorax from the lungs and secrete the pleural fluid. Pleural membranes and fluid let the lungs slide as the thorax changes volume. Lungs are the main terrestrial organs of gas exchange.

q: The rib cage takes part in ventilation.
e: False. It is not true that the rib cage takes part in ventilation. Ventilation is moving air or water across the gas-exchange surface.

q: Ventilation means moving air in and out of the lungs, which requires a difference in air pressure.
e: True. Ventilation means moving air in and out of the lungs, which requires a difference in air pressure. Ventilation is moving air or water across the gas-exchange surface. Lungs are the main terrestrial organs of gas exchange.

q: During inhalation, the external intercostal muscles relax and internal intercostal muscles contract.
e: False. It is not true that during inhalation, the external intercostal muscles relax and internal intercostal muscles contract. Intercostal muscles move the ribs to change thorax volume during breathing.

q: During inhalation, the rib cage causes upward and outward movement.
e: True. During inhalation, the rib cage causes upward and outward movement.

q: During exhalation, the muscles of the diaphragm contract.
e: False. It is not true that during exhalation, the muscles of the diaphragm contract. The diaphragm contracts and flattens to increase thorax volume during inhalation.

q: During inhalation, the diaphragm becomes flattened.
e: True. During inhalation, the diaphragm becomes flattened. The diaphragm contracts and flattens to increase thorax volume during inhalation.

q: During exhalation, the chest decreases in volume and increases in pressure.
e: True. During exhalation, the chest decreases in volume and increases in pressure.
